name: semantic-kernel

facts.description: Integrate cutting-edge LLM technology quickly and easily into your apps

title: Semantic Kernel: Microsoft's SDK for Building LLM-Powered AI Applications
answer: Semantic Kernel is Microsoft's open source SDK, written in C# with an MIT licence, for integrating large language models into applications. It sits between your code and AI services such as OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Google, Mistral, Ollama and Hugging Face, handling chat completion, function calling, plugins and vector store connectors. The one thing to know before adopting it is that several connectors, including Mistral, Google, Hugging Face, Ollama and Bedrock, are still marked experimental and require suppressing experimental warnings.

sections.body: Semantic Kernel is an open source framework from Microsoft, released under the MIT licence and hosted in the microsoft/semantic-kernel repository, which had roughly 28,600 stars at the time of writing. Its stated purpose is to integrate cutting edge LLM technology quickly and easily into applications. It is primarily a C# codebase, though the official documentation also describes Python equivalents for several concepts, such as the kernel_function decorator and the NoneInvoke function choice behavior. It occupies the orchestration layer of the AI stack, sitting above raw model APIs and below your application logic. It does not train models. Instead it connects your code to chat completion services, wraps your own functions as plugins, and manages the back and forth between model and code.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The framework's core job is chat completion, which the documentation describes as the most common AI service added to Semantic Kernel projects and as useful for chat bots and autonomous agents. Its most powerful feature is function calling, where the model can request that your code run. Semantic Kernel serializes available functions and their parameters using JSON schema, sends them with the chat history, invokes whichever functions the model chooses, and feeds the results back until the model returns a message or the maximum iteration count is reached. Plugins extend this to real work, either retrieving data for retrieval augmented generation or automating tasks, and they can be imported from native code, an OpenAPI specification, or an MCP server. Vector store connectors handle serialization of data models to and from database schemas, a feature still marked as preview. It is strongest where you want a model to call your existing APIs and services in a controlled way.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve depends heavily on your starting point. If you already write C# or Python and understand how to call a chat completion API, the basic path is short: add a connector package, register the service on the kernel, and annotate methods with the KernelFunction attribute or kernel_function decorator to expose them. The documentation recommends starting with native code plugins and moving to OpenAPI specifications as an application matures. No mathematics beyond general programming literacy is implied by the material read. The harder parts are conceptual rather than mathematical, particularly the distinction between auto function choice behavior, where the model picks functions, and auto function invocation, where Semantic Kernel runs them, and the reserved parameter names that receive special handling. The official site offers conceptual overviews, code examples, and package installation instructions, which is a reasonable starting point for a beginner but assumes familiarity with the host language.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem is broad on the model side. Chat completion connectors exist for OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Google, Mistral, Hugging Face, Azure AI Inference, Ollama, Amazon Bedrock, and ONNX, with Anthropic models reachable through the Amazon Bedrock platform. Any provider that supports the OpenAI chat completion API, such as LLM Studio, can be used through the OpenAI connector. Plugins can be sourced from native code, OpenAPI documents at versions 2.0 and 3.0 with an attempt to accommodate 3.1 by downgrading, or MCP servers. Plugins work with dependency injection, so database connections and HTTP clients can be injected through a plugin's constructor, and a plugin can be created once and reused across multiple kernel instances or agents. Documentation lives on Microsoft Learn and is detailed, covering function choice behaviors, invocation modes, plugin authoring, and vector store serialization. The repository shows active development, with a last push in October 2026.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Semantic Kernel leans toward both, but with different mechanisms for each. For prototyping, auto function calling is the default, so a developer can register plugins and let the model choose and invoke functions without writing orchestration code. For production control, the framework exposes function choice behaviors Auto, Required, and None, filters over included and excluded plugins and functions, manual invocation where chosen functions are returned to the caller rather than run, and a choice between sequential and concurrent invocation of parallel function calls. Direct serialization for vector stores is described as the best way to ensure full control and optimize performance, at the cost of being specific to one data store. The cost of this flexibility is configuration surface: the documentation notes that specifying both excluded and included plugins, or both excluded and included functions, is not allowed, and that an empty include list has no effect, so disabling function calling requires setting the behavior to None or NoneInvoke.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts available show a Microsoft-maintained project with a substantial star count and an active repository, and the documentation is published on Microsoft Learn, which indicates first party investment. The material read does not name specific adopters or describe hiring demand, so claims about which companies run it in production cannot be grounded here. What can be said is that it is a current, maintained choice rather than a legacy one, and that its C# origin makes it a natural fit for .NET shops. For someone choosing what to learn, the transferable skills are the concepts rather than the API: function calling, plugin design, retrieval augmented generation, and the separation between model choice and code invocation. Those concepts appear across other frameworks, even where the terminology differs.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Semantic Kernel is typically used with C# and .NET, and the documentation also covers Python, so it belongs to the polyglot pattern where a framework offers parallel APIs in more than one language. It is designed to sit alongside model providers rather than replace them, so a project commonly combines it with an OpenAI or Azure OpenAI connector, a vector database through a vector store connector, and existing HTTP APIs exposed as OpenAPI plugins. The documentation notes that not all AI SDKs have an analogous concept to plugins, with most offering only functions or tools, and that Semantic Kernel uses the term functions because they are typically defined as native functions in the codebase. That naming difference matters when reading other frameworks, since tools, actions, and functions often describe the same idea.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: Function calling is only supported by a few AI connectors, and support from small language models is described as still limited, which constrains what the framework can do with cheaper or local models. Several connectors, including Mistral, Google, Hugging Face, Azure AI Inference, Ollama, and Bedrock for Anthropic, are experimental and require suppressing the SKEXP0070 warning, so they should be treated as subject to change. Vector store serialization is marked as preview. OpenAPI plugins with non-unique parameter names are skipped with a warning, and the documentation offers a workaround rather than a full fix. The material read does not state performance benchmarks, memory characteristics, or a formal support policy for the experimental connectors, and it does not describe production deployments by named organisations, so those questions remain open.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
